LEDs are said to last up to 100,000 hours before any marked degradation due to overheating or general usage, although most agree that 50,000 hours is a more reasonable estimate (Evans, 1997; Tetra Tech EM Inc., 2010). The life expectancy of LEDs can double that of HIDs (Josefowicz, 2012). Where LEDs are expected to last in excess of 10 to 15 years, the typical replacement rate of HPS and metal halide lighting systems is every 5.5 years based on an annual usage rate of 4,000 hours (Avrenli et al., 2012). In addition to direct monetary savings associated with replacing conventional systems with LEDs, the ability to easily dim and control LEDs is a notable advantage over other lighting systems. Dimming LED luminaires can result in an additional energy savings of up to 30% (Avrenli et al., 2012). Given the benefits of street lighting and the advancement of lighting technology, street lighting has been widely adopted, sometimes to an excessive level. This, however, leads to a new issue called over-lighting. Over-lighting is the presence of lighting intensity higher than that which is appropriate for a specific activity. It can be caused by lighting unoccupied areas with too much intensity, during daylight hours, or with too few electrical controls. It has been noted that excessive levels of street lighting, in terms of overall brightness, spectral contents, or lighting schedule, may adversely affect a number of factors such as safety, environment, ecology, and energy. 2.1.1 Adaptive Lighting A “smart’ controlled system that dims roadway lighting during periods when traffic and pedestrian activity is low is known as adaptive/smart lighting system (ALS). Finely controlling a lighting system in such a way can not only promote safety during heightened exposure periods but also still consider the effects of sky glow, glare, and light trespass during other times. The concept of adaptive lighting has been effectively applied in a number of cities, such as Cambridge, Massachusetts; Seattle, Washington; and San Jose, California. Adaptive lighting control systems serve to reduce the impact of the lighting system at times when light is less necessary, as well as save a considerable amount of energy and maintenance costs. The adaptive street and roadway lighting systems already installed in cities and towns in the United States have resulted in significant energy savings. Adaptive lighting control is said to achieve savings between 30% and 46% (Escolar et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2013; Muncipal Solid- State Street Lighting Consortium, 2013). In some cases, the effect can be much greater, such as in California. The city of San Jose and University of California – Davis (UC Davis) converted to LEDs and installed adaptive lighting controls, resulting in 84% and 87% energy savings (Muncipal Solid-State Street Lighting Consortium, 2013).
